questions.explain: Applying the Born rule: P(0) = |√(1/3)|² = 1/3 ≈ 0.333 and P(1) = |√(2/3)|² = 2/3 ≈ 0.667. These sum to 1, confirming the state is validly normalized.

questions.q: If measuring |ψ⟩ = √(1/3)|0⟩ + √(2/3)|1⟩ yields outcome 1, what is the qubit's state immediately afterward?
options: Still √(1/3)|0⟩ + √(2/3)|1⟩, unchanged
Exactly |1⟩
A new superposition with P(0)=1/3, P(1)=2/3 reset
Exactly |0⟩, since 1/3 and 2/3 average out
questions.explain: Collapse means the state snaps to exactly the measured outcome's basis state. Getting outcome 1 collapses the qubit to exactly |1⟩, discarding the original amplitude information entirely.

questions.q: What is the key difference between applying the Hadamard gate twice in a row (H·H) versus measuring a qubit while it's in state |+⟩?
options: There is no difference; both processes are identical
H·H is a reversible, deterministic gate sequence (H·H = I); measuring |+⟩ is an irreversible, probabilistic collapse to a definite outcome
H·H is probabilistic while measurement is always deterministic
Measurement can be undone by applying H again, just like H·H can be undone
questions.explain: Applying gates without measuring is fully reversible — H·H returns exactly to the starting state. Measuring collapses the state irreversibly to one definite outcome; no gate can undo that collapse and recover the original superposition.

questions.q: Measuring |0⟩ in the X-basis gives P(+)=P(−)=0.5, and measuring |1⟩ in the X-basis also gives P(+)=P(−)=0.5. What does this pairing demonstrate?
options: That |0⟩ and |1⟩ are actually the same state
That measurement statistics in a single basis can be identical for states that are maximally distinguishable in another basis, so one basis's statistics alone don't fully characterize a state
That the X-basis is an invalid measurement basis for these states
That |0⟩ and |1⟩ cannot be prepared in a lab
questions.explain: |0⟩ and |1⟩ are perfectly distinguishable in the computational basis (P(0)=1 vs. P(0)=0) yet give identical 50/50 statistics in the X-basis — a concrete illustration that single-basis statistics don't capture everything about a state.

questions.q: Why do the |+⟩/|−⟩ computational-basis result and the |0⟩/|1⟩ X-basis result both matter for how chapter 4's Bell-inequality tests work?
options: They don't connect to chapter 4 at all; Bell tests use entirely different concepts

Both show that genuinely different states can share identical single-basis statistics, which is exactly why Bell-inequality tests must compare statistics across multiple deliberately chosen bases to reveal correlations a single basis would hide
They show that only the computational basis is ever useful in practice
They prove that basis choice has no physical effect on measurement outcomes
questions.explain: Both examples establish that a single basis's measurement statistics can fail to distinguish genuinely different states. Bell-inequality tests exploit exactly this by comparing statistics across multiple bases, since the entanglement-revealing correlations only show up that way.
